evidence: Cic. N.D. 1.24; 2.47: cōnum tibi ais et cylindrum et pȳramidem pulchriōrem quam sphaeram vidērī
terms.comment: Greek κῶνος, with a long ō. Cicero names it among the solids; it is also the peak of a helmet and the cone of the cypress (Lewis & Short). The lexicon has it for the ice-cream cone too.

terms.gloss: a cone-shaped post, the turning post of the Circus
evidence: Curt. 8.11: in mētae maximē modum ērēcta
terms.comment: What a Roman saw when he thought of a cone: the mētae at each end of the Circus. So in modum mētae, “cone-shaped”, of a hill or a rock.

evidence: Plin. NH 37.56: turbinātus in mūcrōnem (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Pliny’s adjective, from turbō, a spinning top.

phrases.latin: Hic cōnus īmus lātus est, summus acūtus.
phrases.english: This cone is wide at the bottom and pointed at the top.

phrases.latin: ipse collis est in modum mētae in acūtum cacūmen ā fundō satis lātō fastīgātus
phrases.english: the hill itself is like a cone, rising from a fairly broad base to a sharp peak

phrases.latin: At mihi vel cylindrī vel quadrātī vel cōnī vel pȳramidis vidētur esse fōrmōsior.
phrases.english: But to me the shape of a cylinder, or a cube, or a cone, or a pyramid seems more beautiful.

sources: Lewis & Short: conus · Lewis & Short: meta · Lewis & Short: turbinatus
